DECODE CONFLICT | ONE PILOT. AN AIRBORNE PACK.

In 2026, DARPA and the U.S. Air Force began flying an F 16 modified under the VENOM program with artificial intelligence controlling the aircraft during portions of flight.

The objective is larger than creating an aircraft that can fly itself.

DARPA’s Artificial Intelligence Reinforcements program is testing AI agents that could eventually allow one American pilot to command several autonomous aircraft simultaneously.

Those aircraft could move ahead of the crewed fighter, search for threats, extend sensor coverage, carry electronic warfare systems, create false targets or attack heavily defended positions. The human pilot would retain command authority while artificial intelligence handled navigation, formation management and rapid tactical calculations.

This could fundamentally change how airpower is measured.

Today, planners count aircraft, pilots and available sorties. In a human machine formation, the more important measurement may become how many autonomous aircraft one pilot can direct.

A force of 100 pilots might no longer produce only 100 combat aircraft. It could generate several hundred coordinated airborne platforms performing different missions across the same battlespace.

Decode Conflict Assessment

China may be able to count America’s fighters. It will have greater difficulty calculating the combat power produced when every fighter becomes the command node for an autonomous formation.

The American pilot is not disappearing.

The pilot is being promoted from aircraft operator to airborne battle manager.

The future of air dominance may not be one fighter against another.

It may be one American pilot arriving with an entire pack.

Sources: DARPA and the U.S. Air Force.
